papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When applied thoughtfully it can preserve most of a teacher model’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute; when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design it enables robust, production-ready deployments. However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case failures. Best results arise from integrating distillation into a broader compression pipeline with methods tailored to the target task and constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable set of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. When combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and tailored to task and data constraints, KD unlocks deployment on latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained platforms while supporting modalities from language to vision and multimodal systems. However, KD is not automatic: careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors (bias, rare-token degradation) are required for responsible, robust outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Mechanisms, and Design Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and training protocols (offline teacher, online mutual learning, self-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-free schemes) and can be integrated with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. When carefully designed, KD not only approximates teacher performance but can act as a regularizer that improves generalization; however, reliable outcomes require attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data selection, layer alignment, and privacy or domain constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It enables deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints across vision, language, and multimodal tasks while supporting robustness and transfer when combined with task-aware design. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and data quality, architectural alignment, and complementary compression techniques, and it can propagate teacher biases and fail on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena unless mitigated.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Universal Tool for Model Compression and Practical Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique that enables model compression, deployment efficiency, and task- or domain-specific adaptation across a wide range of deep learning settings. Empirical work shows KD can reduce memory and compute with small accuracy loss, enable low-precision inference, compress specialized generative or multi-modal models, and provide routes to interpretability and data- or privacy-constrained scenarios. Best results arise when KD is adapted to the task (choice of objectives, teacher ensembles, data augmentation, or data-free strategies) and when student architectures or training protocols explicitly account for heterogeneity between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature collectively reports about knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques: commonly used distillation objectives and training protocols, empirical patterns of when and how KD helps across modalities, practical constraints and failure modes (data availability, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency/structured outputs, privacy and bias transfer), and targeted solutions (data-free/zero-shot distillation, teacher engineering, multi-teacher and curriculum schemes, and combinations with pruning/quantization and architecture search). The goal is to give a concise map of methods, observed trade-offs, and open problems for researchers and practitioners working on compressing or adapting large models for resource- or deployment-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring information from large, often multi-modal or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD has been adapted into many forms — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and offline protocols, and data-free or zero-shot schemes — and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance in many settings when teacher quality, student capacity, and appropriate data or synthesis strategies are addressed; theoretical and empirical analyses highlight KD’s role both as knowledge transfer and as a regularizer. Despite broad success, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or heterogeneous data, and propagation of teacher artifacts; current best practice is to treat KD as one element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are now core tools for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. The literature has expanded far beyond simple logits matching to include feature- and representation-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, and tight integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates broad applicability across modalities (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and generative models) and deployment contexts (edge devices, federated systems, and data-constrained settings). The main practical challenges are (1) choosing what and how to distill for a given task and student architecture, (2) coping with limited or unavailable original training data, (3) avoiding transfer of teacher weaknesses (e.g., biases or low-frequency degradation), and (4) co-designing distillation with other compression primitives and hardware constraints. Progress comes from combining representational objectives, layer-mapping strategies, task-aware teacher selection, and safeguards (privacy or fairness) appropriate to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller students. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals, synthetic data) and in protocol (offline, online, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, data-free variants). Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and graph domains demonstrate that distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is carefully designed and combined with complementary compression techniques; however, success depends on factors such as teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes including bias transfer and degraded performance on rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses pretraining, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for privacy and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.'}, {'author': 'Peterson', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation', 'abstract': 'Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.'}, {'author': 'Martin', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. Best results arise from integrating distillation into a broader compression pipeline with methods tailored to the target task and constraints.'}, {'author': 'Bernard', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.'}, {'author': 'Kelley', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). When combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and tailored to task and data constraints, KD unlocks deployment on latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained platforms while supporting modalities from language to vision and multimodal systems. However, KD is not automatic: careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors (bias, rare-token degradation) are required for responsible, robust outcomes.'}, {'author': 'Aguilar', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.'}, {'author': 'Cortez', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments."}, {'author': 'Hall', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models', 'abstract': 'Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.'}, {'author': 'Walls', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.'}, {'author': 'Wong', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.'}, {'author': 'Jackson', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Mechanisms, and Design Principles', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models into smaller, deployable students. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.'}, {'author': 'Cohen', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques."}, {'author': 'Cameron', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models', 'abstract': 'Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and data quality, architectural alignment, and complementary compression techniques, and it can propagate teacher biases and fail on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena unless mitigated.'}, {'author': 'May', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. The goal is to give a concise map of methods, observed trade-offs, and open problems for researchers and practitioners working on compressing or adapting large models for resource- or deployment-constrained settings.'}, {'author': 'Hodges', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Despite broad success, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or heterogeneous data, and propagation of teacher artifacts; current best practice is to treat KD as one element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline.'}, {'author': 'Walters', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are now core tools for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers.
