papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential Tool for Practical Deep Learning — Potentials, Pitfalls, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into indispensable tools for deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained, privacy-sensitive, and latency-critical environments. Across modalities—vision, language, speech, and generation—KD enables smaller or heterogeneous models to approach teacher performance, improves interpretability in specific settings, and reduces communication costs in distributed learning. However, distillation is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher biases, suffer under data heterogeneity, and interact subtly with training practices. Careful choices—selective sample usage, multi- or self-distillation, architectural adapters, annealing strategies, and privacy-aware generative replay—help realize KD's benefits while mitigating its limitations. This paper synthesizes evidence from applied and theoretical work to argue that KD should be treated as a central engineering primitive, accompanied by the practices needed for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking model size and latency while preserving performance across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation, and federated settings. Research has expanded beyond the original logits-matching paradigm into feature mimicking, many-to-many layer mapping, teacher engineering, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights important interactions between data complexity, teacher strength, inductive bias, and augmentation strategies, and identifies practical challenges including model-heterogeneity, data heterogeneity, and the need for robust data-free methods. The field increasingly emphasizes not only how to distill but also what to distill (logits, features, inter-class relations, view- or task-specific knowledge) and how to adapt distillation to application constraints (privacy, federated settings, domain shifts, resource budgets).

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When adapted to task, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprint, and improved adaptability across domains and modalities. However, KD is a family of techniques rather than a single algorithm: best outcomes arise from combining distillation with complementary methods (e.g., pruning, architecture search, curriculum design, data synthesis) and from explicitly addressing challenges such as imperfect teachers, domain shift, privacy, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core method for producing compact, efficient models from large deep networks across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD delivers substantial inference and memory savings while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, enabling deployment in latency-, power-, and privacy-constrained settings. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections (biases, distributional blind spots) and faces practical constraints (data mismatch, teacher–student capacity gaps, limited-data regimes). Effective use of KD therefore requires matching objectives, data strategies, and architectures to deployment goals and complementing distillation with pruning, quantization, or privacy-aware protocols when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Mechanisms, and Design Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and training protocols (offline teacher, online mutual learning, self-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-free schemes) and can be integrated with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. When carefully designed, KD not only approximates teacher performance but can act as a regularizer that improves generalization; however, reliable outcomes require attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data selection, layer alignment, and privacy or domain constraints.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Multifaceted Toolbox with Clear Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practically essential approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains and can improve generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods, but it is not a single recipe: success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and constraints such as privacy or heterogeneous deployment hardware. Practical KD pipelines therefore treat distillation as a configurable toolkit—selecting objectives, data strategies, and auxiliary interventions (e.g., pruning, quantization, teacher adaptation, or student-aware design) that match the task and constraints—while explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Salazar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broad, practically driven family of methods that transfer predictive behavior, internal representations, or structured information from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, channel- and layer-wise objectives, self- and multi-teacher designs, data-free and few-shot protocols, and adversarial or generator-based data synthesis. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data and training practices, distillation often preserves much of the teacher's performance and can add functional guarantees (robustness, low-precision accuracy, privacy-aware releases). Key limitations include dependence on teacher quality, student capacity and architectural alignment, distributional mismatch or limited data, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or biases, motivating continued work on principled objectives, data strategies, and deployment-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression, Transfer, and Robustification in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a technique for shrinking models: it is a flexible paradigm that enables model compression, domain and modality transfer, continual adaptation, and improved interpretability and fairness. A range of strategies — from many-to-many layer alignment and feature mimicking to data-free synthesis, online peer teaching, and augmentation-aware distillation — make KD applicable across tasks (classification, generation, detection, ASR, GANs) and settings (distributed training, privacy-constrained, few-shot, multi-task). However, practical use requires careful design choices (what to transfer, how to match teacher and student, and how to handle teacher–student discrepancy and label-processing artifacts). When applied with methods matched to these considerations, KD consistently yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance while unlocking deployment and research scenarios otherwise infeasible for large, monolithic networks.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and highly practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD techniques range from simple soft-target matching to representation- and task-aware objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-augmentation and data-free protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is effective across modalities and tasks but is not a silver bullet: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and explicit handling of biases and distribution shift. Treated as a core component within an integrated compression pipeline and designed with task constraints in mind, KD yields reliable tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity for deployment in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks and specialized settings (e.g., 3D detection, ranking, medical imaging), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or synthetic alternatives are used; KD is most effective when used as a configurable component combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware training strategies.

papers_seen.author: Contreras
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency and can transfer task-relevant structure from teachers to students, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices of what to transfer, teacher selection, data and optimization strategies, and complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires attention to robustness, fairness, privacy, and teacher–student co-design.

Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core set of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and layer correspondences; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search. KD supports many practical settings — including data-limited, data-free, few-shot, federated, and cross-modal scenarios — but its effectiveness depends on choices such as which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Ongoing directions include principled theory for transfer objectives, robust and private distillation, and task-aware designs for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to reduce the resource footprint of large neural networks while preserving performance. The literature surveys a range of approaches — from vanilla teacher-student soft-target transfers to layer-wise, attention- and channel-wise methods, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with pruning and adversarial training — and demonstrates successful applications across NLP, speech, vision, graph, and multimodal problems. Empirical results show effective speedups and parameter reductions with modest accuracy loss; theoretical and empirical analyses also connect KD to label-smoothing and regularization effects that can improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Across vision and language, researchers have explored teacher-student training, intermediate-layer alignment, data- and label-space manipulations, data-free or few-shot settings, and architecture-aware compression. These techniques can preserve much of a teacher's performance while yielding smaller, faster models, and they can be combined with pruning, architecture search, or ensemble compression. KD also intersects with concerns about fairness, generalization, and privacy, and its effectiveness depends on design choices such as the form of distilled targets, data augmentation, and the match between teacher, student, and task.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for compressing large or ensemble deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of task performance. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure), how distillation is arranged (offline, online, multi- or self-distillation), and how data is used or synthesized; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptations, KD supports deployments under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD produces strong empirical gains across modalities (vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, and generative models) but requires task-aware design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, coping with limited or mismatched data, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors—to be reliable in production.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD variants include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structures, ensembling multiple teachers, adversarial and data-free distillation, and student- or task-aware curricula. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted for settings with limited or private data, federated training, and non‑standard outputs (e.g., generative or structured prediction). Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Ongoing research focuses on principled objectives, robust and private distillation, and task‑aware architectures for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, the data used for distillation, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines — combining logits and feature objectives, projector modules, multi‑teacher or teacher‑adaptive designs, and data‑aware schedules — yields the most reliable results in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: State of the Art, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated set of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. KD variants and complementary compression methods enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative tasks. Success requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teachers and students, how to handle limited or private data, and how to integrate distillation with pretraining and other compression methods. Remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, preserving low-frequency behaviors, and robust data-free or federated distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has established itself as a primary mechanism for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate features and representations, and they are readily combined with quantization, pruning, ensembling, and domain-adaptation techniques. While KD frequently yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance degradation—and sometimes performance improvements—its success depends on careful method selection, teacher quality, data and sample selection, and complementary engineering such as layer alignment or teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking model size and latency while preserving performance across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation, and federated settings. Research has expanded beyond the original logits-matching paradigm into feature mimicking, many-to-many layer mapping, teacher engineering, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights important interactions between data complexity, teacher strength, inductive bias, and augmentation strategies, and identifies practical challenges including model-heterogeneity, data heterogeneity, and the need for robust data-free methods. The field increasingly emphasizes not only how to distill but also what to distill (logits, features, inter-class relations, view- or task-specific knowledge) and how to adapt distillation to application constraints (privacy, federated settings, domain shifts, resource budgets).

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool: Integrating Distillation with Representation, Data, and Architecture Strategies for Robust Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, more deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient to meet real-world deployment constraints: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention), and access to or synthesis of suitable training data. Best results arise when KD is embedded in an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level matching, projector or layer-mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Careful attention to optimization, robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors is required to avoid propagating teacher errors and to produce reliable compact models for downstream applications.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression trick into a broad set of techniques that enable efficient deployment, cross-modal transfer, federated and privacy-preserving learning, and improved generalization across domains. Empirical results across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs) show that KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining most of the teacher performance. However, the success of KD depends on careful choices — teacher quality, what to distill (outputs, features, internal representations), data availability and augmentation, and the loss or alignment mechanism — and recent work proposes multiple refinements (multi-teacher schemes, adversarial critics, projector modules, teacher-free variants) that mitigate known failure modes. The balance of empirical evidence and theoretical analyses indicates that KD is both practically indispensable for many compression tasks and a fertile area for research on how knowledge should be measured, transferred, and regularized.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.
