papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple teacher-to-student logit matching into a broad toolkit for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains. Modern KD transfers soft targets, intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, or synthesized data; it operates in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency, but success depends on teacher quality, capacity matching, data/augmentation strategy, and careful design of objectives and layer mappings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, applications, and practical recommendations documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Herring
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, many-to-many layer mappings, projector-based feature transforms, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis — enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Successful application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle data availability and privacy, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. Remaining research challenges include principled theory for objective selection, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation mimicking, relational or attention-map transfer, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and recommendation settings. Empirical and theoretical work demonstrates substantial practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability when KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping), but success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objective design; remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, distribution shift, rare-token performance, and bias or privacy leakage.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable models across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When paired with complementary techniques—layer mapping, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, pruning/quantization, and curriculum or online schemes—KD yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance while supporting privacy-conscious and latency-constrained deployments. Remaining limits around data availability, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional mismatch can be mitigated by choosing appropriate distillation targets and architectures and by combining KD with targeted engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, detection, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—enable substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, data strategy, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression (e.g., pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Practical deployments use task-aware adaptations, confidence- or curriculum-based weighting, and privacy- or federated-aware designs; remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, rare-output transfer, and principled theory for optimal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central and Versatile but Insufficient Alone — Practical Position and Best Practices for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative settings. KD reliably improves student performance when teacher quality, the form of transferred signals, and data/augmentation strategies are chosen to match the task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not sufficient by itself: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful data or augmentation strategies, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations. This article argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all, and it highlights empirical evidence, mechanisms, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring knowledge from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. Beyond straightforward parameter reduction, KD is used to improve student generalization, robustness, interpretability, domain adaptation, continual learning, and to enable deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a wide variety of KD objectives (logit/soft-label matching, feature imitation, relational losses), training protocols (multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial or zero-shot data generation, teacher-free/self-distillation), and application-specific adaptations (detection, retrieval, GANs, speech, lipreading, 3D vision, recommender systems, and NLP). Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance and in some cases surpass teachers on efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, but raise challenges including heterogeneous teacher-student alignment, data availability, preserving low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and transferring robustness and domain-general knowledge.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a logits-matching trick into a broad, practical framework for shrinking and adapting large models while retaining much of their performance. Modern KD techniques include soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, online and distributed formulations, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Across vision, language, recommendation, and domain-adaptation settings, KD is most effective when combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, pruning, quantization, curriculum or online training, and task-aware losses). Despite strong empirical successes, practitioners must attend to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and domain mismatch; many current research directions focus on robust, privacy-preserving, and data-limited distillation for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a broadly useful means to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students so that compressed models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is adapted to the problem: what to transfer (logits, features, attention), which data to use or synthesize, how to weight multiple teachers or imperfect supervision, and how to integrate complementary compression techniques. However, KD is neither automatic nor sufficient on its own: careful, task-aware design and combination with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies are required to realize reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central and Versatile but Insufficient Alone — Practical Position and Best Practices for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Power, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD variants transfer information via logits, intermediate features, or data synthesized from teachers; they can also be combined with privacy or fairness measures. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, dataset mismatches, and design choices (what to mimic, which layers, how to align teacher and student) strongly affect outcomes. Careful method selection—feature vs. logit supervision, layer alignment, projector usage, sample selection, and teacher adaptation—enables consistent gains while meeting constraints like limited data, privacy, or fairness.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for compressing large or ensemble deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of task performance. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure), how distillation is arranged (offline, online, multi- or self-distillation), and how data is used or synthesized; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptations, KD supports deployments under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD produces strong empirical gains across modalities (vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, and generative models) but requires task-aware design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, coping with limited or mismatched data, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors—to be reliable in production.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones across modalities and tasks. The field encompasses diverse mechanisms — from soft-target supervision and feature imitation to contrastive and adversarial schemes — and integrates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work highlights when and why different formulations help, how to handle limited or absent teacher data, and which practical choices matter for robustness, fairness, and domain-specific demands.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more complex teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet constraints of latency, memory, privacy, or deployment. The field presents a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free), and architecture-aware adaptations that are frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and control shows distilled students can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed; however, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts, and challenges in reliably transferring robustness, low-frequency behaviors, and fairness. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox within an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals and data strategies according to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across logits-based soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, layer-mapping or projector modules, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or federated protocols, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical results show KD can sometimes improve generalization and enable deployment under privacy or resource constraints, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and careful design choices about what and how to transfer. Combining KD with complementary techniques (augmentation, curriculum learning, pruning, quantization, architecture search) and tailoring the distillation signals to task and deployment constraints yields the most reliable practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Herring
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, many-to-many layer mappings, projector-based feature transforms, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis — enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Successful application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle data availability and privacy, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. Remaining research challenges include principled theory for objective selection, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Shelton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical framework for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. A broad family of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/zero-shot) has been developed and combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and neural architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of data (real or synthetic), and design choices about what and how to transfer; common failure modes include teacher error propagation, teacher–student mismatch, optimization gaps, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolkit—selecting signals, mappings, and curricula appropriate to the task and constraints and combining KD with other compression strategies and safeguards for privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or specialized students to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use a range of objectives — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational losses, adversarially generated supervision, and teacher-free/self-distillation variants — often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective in many settings (supervised, self-supervised, online, federated, and data-free), but its success depends on choices about what information to transfer, teacher quality and alignment to the student, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and the complement of compression techniques used. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both why distillation helps (regularization, privileged information, smoother targets) and when it struggles (capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena), suggesting hybrid pipelines and task-aware designs as practical routes forward.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD methods vary by what is transferred (teacher logits, internal representations, attention, relational structure), how layers are aligned or projected, and how data constraints (limited access, privacy, or distribution shift) are handled. Empirical work demonstrates that combining output-level and representation-level objectives, using layer-mapping or projector modules, and adapting training data or curricula yields the best trade-offs between compactness and accuracy. Despite wide success, effective distillation requires careful choices about teacher quality, distilled signals, sample selection, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster students to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and compute. A diverse set of distillation targets and training paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention-map imitation, layer-wise mapping, adversarial and data-free generation of surrogate examples, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and integration with architecture search or pruning—have been developed and adapted to vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of the teacher's accuracy (and in some settings improves generalization or robustness) when combined with task-aware choices of signals to transfer, data augmentation, and teacher-student design; remaining gaps and failure modes are linked to teacher quality, data availability and distribution shift, heterogeneous architectures, and fairness or robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool: Integrating Distillation with Representation, Data, and Architecture Strategies for Robust Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, more deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient to meet real-world deployment constraints: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention), and access to or synthesis of suitable training data. Best results arise when KD is embedded in an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level matching, projector or layer-mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Careful attention to optimization, robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors is required to avoid propagating teacher errors and to produce reliable compact models for downstream applications.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.
