papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performance deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across computer vision, generative modeling, 3D rendering, graph learning, and natural language processing, researchers employ a range of distillation paradigms — including teacher-student soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models — to produce smaller, faster, or more interpretable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. Practical concerns such as limited or unavailable training data, domain shifts, adversarial robustness, and the need for interpretable or low-precision models have driven specific adaptations of KD. Empirical results across tasks show that (1) distillation can greatly reduce model size or runtime with small accuracy loss, (2) internal- and feature-level matching often improves transfer beyond logits-only approaches, and (3) novel protocols (e.g., ensemble teachers, generative pseudo-replay, many-to-many layer alignment) expand KD applicability to privacy-sensitive, multimodal, and generation tasks.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers capabilities of large models into smaller ones via indirect supervision. Methods vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and practical constraints (limited data, privacy, cross-distribution generalization, modality mismatch). Empirical work across speech, vision, language, retrieval, graph, generative modeling, and medical imaging shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while gaining resource efficiency; theoretical analyses and diagnostic studies clarify mechanisms and guide designs such as projector layers, many-to-many layer mapping, and curriculum or data-augmentation strategies. Remaining challenges include distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of inductive biases, and principled layer-to-layer alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and federated settings, KD variants transfer soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, contrastive signals, synthetic inputs, or ensemble outputs. KD can enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, improve student generalization, support privacy-preserving workflows, and interact fruitfully with pruning and low-precision numerics. However, the benefits depend strongly on data availability, teacher quality, architecture alignment, and training protocols; important failure modes include optimization gaps, preserved or amplified teacher biases, degraded rare-token behavior, and teacher inference cost. The literature provides many practical strategies—feature- and layer-wise matching, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial or data-free sample generation, student-aware teacher design, and hardware-aware co-design—to mitigate these limitations and extend KD to specialized tasks such as federated learning, continual/lifelong learning, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. The literature has expanded from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolbox that includes intermediate-feature matching, attention and relational objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware search. Empirical work shows that with task-aware objectives and careful handling of teacher-student mismatches, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks, though important challenges remain around data scarcity, teacher imperfection, capacity mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, researchers have extended KD beyond soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, online and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. Practical success depends on teacher quality and student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthetic-data strategies, and combinations with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include principled understanding of when particular signals help, handling heterogeneous or non-iid data in federated settings, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and reliably scaling distillation in large distributed systems.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while often preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, objective design, and architecture alignment. To realize KD's benefits in production and research, practitioners should treat distillation as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits and representation matching, data-aware schedules or synthesis, and complementary compression methods—while applying targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD enables practical deployment across modalities and constrained settings, but its success depends on careful design choices, complementary compression primitives, and explicit safeguards against transferred errors and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal domains, a diverse set of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational structure) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, data‑free or self‑distillation) have been developed. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover much of a teacher’s performance while enabling lower latency, reduced memory use, and new deployment modes; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design of the transfer objective. Practical pipelines commonly pair KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task‑aware procedures (layer mapping, curriculum, teacher adaptation) to meet deployment constraints. Important open problems include robust transfer under distribution shift and data scarcity, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, principled automated design for heterogeneous student architectures, and privacy‑aware or data‑free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Cross-Domain Argument for Practical, Responsible, and Multi-Modal Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for deploying modern deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across vision, language, graph, and generative domains, distillation methods can preserve most of a teacher's performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication. Best results come from (a) matching appropriate internal representations (layer mapping, attention, many-to-many mappings), (b) designing teachers or multi-teacher schemes that are student-aware, and (c) combining distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, NAS, adversarial training, federated schemes). However, practitioners must be mindful of failure modes—bias amplification, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and gaps when no training data are available—and adopt targeted mitigations such as task-adaptive compression, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, and data-free or privacy-preserving distillation when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller or more efficient ones, reducing computational cost and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings. Approaches vary in what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate representations, feature maps, attention or decision-boundary information), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, ensemble distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving setups), and how training data or augmentation is used. Empirical results across computer vision, speech/lipreading, retrieval, translation, reading comprehension, CTR prediction, federated learning, GANs, NAS, and Transformer compression show that appropriate combination of distillation objective, data strategy, and model design can yield large gains in efficiency with modest or no loss in accuracy. Practical factors that shape success include teacher strength and mismatch to the student, the complexity of distilled data, the role of pre-training for compact models, targeted selection or augmentation of distillation samples, and orthogonal compression techniques such as structured pruning.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transfer information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Approaches vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or decision-boundary information), by whether original training data are available, and by whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work across vision, multimodal, speech, and natural language tasks shows that careful choices of transfer targets, loss formulations, teacher ensembles, and training schedules can yield compact models that approach — and in some cases match or exceed — teacher performance while enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties that prevent perfect belief matching, distribution-shift and heterogeneity issues in federated or data-free settings, and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, structured prediction, and language tasks—KD variants (logit transfer, feature- and attention-matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols) provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as architecture search, pruning, low-precision numerics, or privacy mechanisms, distillation enables robust deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive platforms. However, distillation outcomes depend on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student alignment, and design choices for objectives and training pipelines; tailored practices are therefore needed to realize KD's full potential and avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool: Integrating Distillation with Representation, Data, and Architecture Strategies for Robust Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, more deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient to meet real-world deployment constraints: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention), and access to or synthesis of suitable training data. Best results arise when KD is embedded in an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level matching, projector or layer-mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Careful attention to optimization, robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors is required to avoid propagating teacher errors and to produce reliable compact models for downstream applications.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. KD spans logits- and feature-based transfers, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and task-specific adaptations. Its strengths include enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, improving latency and memory footprints, and supporting privacy- or data-constrained scenarios. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, data availability and mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, architectural alignment, and deployment heterogeneity require complementary techniques and task-aware engineering to realize reliable, robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones into a broad set of methods that address efficiency, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness, fairness, and cross-modal transfer. By moving beyond simple logits matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher schemes, data-free and few-shot settings, and meta-learned teachers, distillation can both preserve performance and add functional guarantees (e.g., robustness, fairness) that are crucial for real-world deployment. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be considered a foundational component of model compression pipelines and of strategies for adapting large pre-trained models to constrained, specialized, or sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A synthesis of methods, evidence, and practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, multifaceted toolkit for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. The field unifies a set of objectives (soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational/contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, self- and mutual-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-annealed schedules), and data strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis, adversarial generation) that, when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable effective deployment across vision, language, generative modelling, and domain- and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical evidence demonstrates strong gains when distillation is matched to student capacity, teacher quality, and appropriate data/augmentation strategies, but persistent challenges remain in data-scarce, privacy-sensitive, domain-shift, and heterogeneous-architecture regimes.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Practices, Mechanisms, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of methods for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD techniques vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure), how teachers and students are arranged (offline, online, ensemble, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers), and whether distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD succeeds across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks but is context-sensitive: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, loss and mapping design, and deployment constraints. Practical distillation therefore requires task- and deployment-aware choices, and often additional techniques (data augmentation, feature projectors, adversarial objectives, or data-free synthesis) to close the gap to teachers while avoiding transferred errors or degraded handling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a practical, flexible approach to compressing large neural models into resource-efficient students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks — from language and retrieval to vision, generation, and graph learning — distillation techniques enable trade-offs between accuracy, compute, and memory that make deployment feasible on constrained hardware. However, the effectiveness of distillation depends strongly on the distillation objective, the information transferred (probabilities, internal representations, or structured signals), availability of original data, and care to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, architecture search, low-precision training, or curriculum strategies), distillation can yield compact models that approach or sometimes even exceed teacher performance while meeting practical latency and size constraints.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-target (logit) supervision to representation- and layer-wise alignment—and integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or curriculum strategies. Empirical evidence across vision, language, generative models, and retrieval shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher accuracy and can add benefits such as improved generalization or interpretability when applied carefully. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, optimization choices, and explicit handling of teacher biases and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component in a broader compression pipeline, chosen and tuned to the task, data availability, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and sometimes improve robustness or task adaptation. A diverse toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and generative data-free techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and selective or meta-learned teaching—and empirical and theoretical work clarifies when and why these choices succeed or fail. Practical deployment requires matching the distilled signal to student capacity and task constraints, handling data- or architecture-mismatch, and explicitly addressing bias and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task- and Data-Aware Knowledge Distillation: Principles, Pitfalls, and Practical Extensions for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its practical success across vision, language, graph, and generative models depends not only on the generic teacher→student paradigm but on task-aware selection of transferred information, choices about data access (including data-free and privacy-preserving variants), and the use of auxiliary techniques (adversarial training, ensembling, pruning, and architecture search). When these dimensions are addressed explicitly, distillation can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while offering improved robustness, interpretability, or resource-efficiency. However, naive distillation can fail due to optimization difficulties, domain shift, and heterogeneous teacher-student mismatches, so practitioners must adopt targeted strategies that consider the learning objective, available data, and student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are essential for deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints. Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and NLP shows that combining sensible pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals (outputs and internal representations), appropriate training data or augmentation, and dynamic teacher-student strategies yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Complementary techniques — online or mutual distillation, data-free and federated distillation, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation — further extend applicability to privacy-constrained, multi-domain, and large-scale training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-specific tasks. KD’s flexibility—transferring soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive signals—lets practitioners tailor compression to hardware, privacy, or accuracy constraints. Empirical evidence shows that when distillation is designed task- and capacity-aware and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or progressive module replacement), students can recover much of teacher performance and gain robustness or interpretability in particular settings. At the same time, KD is not automatic: teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, teacher–student mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases require careful protocols (sample selection, layer mapping, objective weighting, and privacy- or robustness-aware extensions). I argue KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful and broadly applicable, but demand-aware and paired with best practices to realize its potential reliably.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. The literature converges on a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure, decision-boundary samples), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, teacher-annealing, self- or online-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data approaches), and architecture-aware adaptations (many-to-many layer mapping, projector adapters, and combinations with pruning/quantization). Empirical studies across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and generative tasks show distilled students can recover much teacher performance and sometimes yield superior efficiency–accuracy trade-offs; nonetheless, open problems remain around data scarcity and privacy, teacher–student mismatch, preserving low-frequency behaviors, and transferring robustness and fairness properties.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical set of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from larger or otherwise stronger models (teachers) to smaller or more constrained models (students). KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, speech, graph learning, reinforcement and lifelong learning—yielding work on algorithmic variants (self-distillation, multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial, relational and loss-function innovations), data- and privacy-aware designs, and hardware-aware/low-precision deployments. Empirical work demonstrates KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance, but theoretical and optimization limits remain: students often cannot perfectly match teachers and training/data choices matter greatly. Practical advances address these limits through better supervision signals, input-side design (data augmentation), alternate discrepancy measures, and privacy/communication constraints. The field continues to move toward more efficient, fair, private and domain-robust distilled models suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Pragmatic, Multifaceted Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a multifaceted framework—covering logits, intermediate representations, feature maps, sample selection, and data-side interventions—KD enables deployments under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Mechanisms, and Design Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and training protocols (offline teacher, online mutual learning, self-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-free schemes) and can be integrated with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. When carefully designed, KD not only approximates teacher performance but can act as a regularizer that improves generalization; however, reliable outcomes require attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data selection, layer alignment, and privacy or domain constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges

It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports domain adaptation and privacy-aware workflows, and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Real-world deployments therefore require KD to be treated as a configurable component within a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data availability, robustness, and fairness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: The Efficacy and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into efficient students across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and reinforcement learning). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while offering substantial inference speedups and parameter reductions, and can be enhanced by targeted techniques (data augmentation, intermediate-layer matching, multi-teacher schedules, contrastive objectives, and meta-learning). However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends strongly on distillation procedure, data complexity, teacher–student alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation objectives and data strategies that address robustness, limited-data regimes, privacy/federation, and modality-specific needs.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, the data used for distillation, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines — combining logits and feature objectives, projector modules, multi‑teacher or teacher‑adaptive designs, and data‑aware schedules — yields the most reliable results in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output.
