papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation mimicking, relational or attention-map transfer, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and recommendation settings. Empirical and theoretical work demonstrates substantial practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability when KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping), but success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objective design; remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, distribution shift, rare-token performance, and bias or privacy leakage.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the capabilities of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Order, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: I argue that knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first-order technique for compressing and adapting deep models for practical deployment in vision and language systems. KD's flexibility—supporting logits, intermediate features, relational signals, online/multi-teacher regimes, and data-free variants—lets practitioners address latency, memory, on-device inference, privacy, and domain adaptation constraints. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of transfer signals, data availability (or synthetic data methods), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Accordingly, KD should be used as a configurable toolkit combined with task-aware design, auxiliary compression methods, and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and sometimes improve robustness or task adaptation. A diverse toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and generative data-free techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and selective or meta-learned teaching—and empirical and theoretical work clarifies when and why these choices succeed or fail. Practical deployment requires matching the distilled signal to student capacity and task constraints, handling data- or architecture-mismatch, and explicitly addressing bias and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but computationally expensive neural networks in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more specialized ones. This synthesis summarizes methods for transferring output-level and internal representations, architectural and layer-wise strategies for compression, training variants (e.g., self-supervised, adversarial, few-shot, online, and federated settings), and applications across NLP, vision, generative models, graph learning, and distributed systems. It highlights empirical findings on when distillation is most effective, techniques to preserve or improve robustness and fairness, and practical strategies for heterogeneous and latency-sensitive deployments. Gaps and recurring challenges are identified to guide future work.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD has matured into a toolbox that includes logit- and feature-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free and adversarial generation, online and multi-teacher schemes, and task-aware layer alignment. Its effectiveness in reducing parameters, latency, and memory—often with modest performance loss—makes KD a core first-line method for deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, bias transfer, limited or private data) that require task-aware protocols, complementary compression techniques, and targeted research into robustness, privacy, and automated teacher/student design.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so that students achieve improved accuracy, latency, or resource use while retaining much of teacher behavior. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, internal features, relational structure, or contrastive/global representations), how supervision is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and how distillation is combined with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows substantial gains across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and generative models, but limitations remain around data availability, teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency information transfer, privacy constraints, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of techniques for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving task performance. Across vision, language, and multimodal domains, KD has evolved beyond logits-only supervision into rich protocols that match intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized data or generator-based replay. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful objective and layer alignment. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, practical recommendations, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but its success depends on careful choices about what information is transferred, how teachers and students are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as the central element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a sole solution.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment across domains and modalities. When designed with task-awareness (choice of distilled signal, teacher selection, and training scheme), KD can preserve accuracy while materially improving latency, memory, and privacy characteristics. Best results arise from combining multiple KD techniques (logit, feature, layer-wise, adversarial, and ensemble-based) chosen to match the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical Tool That Requires Context-Aware Integration
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable technique for transferring behavior from large teacher models to compact students across vision, language, generative, and distributed settings. However, KD is not a silver bullet; its success depends on teacher quality, choice of distilled signals, available data, and optimization procedures. For practical, high-fidelity compression, KD should be treated as a core component of a broader pipeline that includes pre-training of compact architectures, careful layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher or meta-learned teaching strategies, data-aware augmentation or synthesis, and complementary compression methods such as pruning or quantization.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, structured prediction, and language tasks—KD variants (logit transfer, feature- and attention-matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols) provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as architecture search, pruning, low-precision numerics, or privacy mechanisms, distillation enables robust deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive platforms. However, distillation outcomes depend on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student alignment, and design choices for objectives and training pipelines; tailored practices are therefore needed to realize KD's full potential and avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Practical Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving functionality. Beyond simple size reduction, distillation enables device deployment, privacy-preserving releases, latency reduction, ensemble compression, improved low-precision accuracy, and better generalization when combined with complementary techniques. Successful deployment requires matching distillation method to problem structure (e.g., graphs, vision-language, transformers), addressing teacher-induced biases, and adopting strategies such as data-free synthesis, task-aware layer selection, relational objectives, and teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-target (logit) supervision to representation- and layer-wise alignment—and integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or curriculum strategies. Empirical evidence across vision, language, generative models, and retrieval shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher accuracy and can add benefits such as improved generalization or interpretability when applied carefully. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, optimization choices, and explicit handling of teacher biases and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component in a broader compression pipeline, chosen and tuned to the task, data availability, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or richer models (teachers) into smaller, more efficient models (students). KD methods range from matching teacher output distributions to aligning internal representations and using synthesized or privatized data; they are effective across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks and are commonly integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while improving inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against propagating undesirable teacher properties. Current practice treats KD as a configurable component of wider compression pipelines rather than a single algorithm, and several methodological extensions and safeguards have been proposed to address its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative settings. KD reliably improves student performance when teacher quality, the form of transferred signals, and data/augmentation strategies are chosen to match the task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not sufficient by itself: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful data or augmentation strategies, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations. This article argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all, and it highlights empirical evidence, mechanisms, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Adaptation, Privacy, and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression recipe: it is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from one set of models to another. KD enables production of compact, fast models that retain much of a larger model's performance, and it can be adapted to address domain shift, limited or private data, modality-specific constraints, and even fairness or robustness objectives. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for transferring predictive behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, efficient students. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods extend beyond logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention-level transfer, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD can yield compact models that retain much teacher performance, but success depends on careful selection of what and how to transfer, data availability, and the match between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Practical Necessity, Limitations, and a Consolidated Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high‑performing deep models in resource‑constrained settings across vision, speech, recommendation, graph, and language tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: teacher inference cost, data mismatches introduced by distillation, low‑frequency token degradation, privacy considerations, and heterogeneous deployment constraints each demand tailored remedies. Combining complementary strategies — multi‑teacher distillation, student‑aware teacher design, projector/feature adaptation, self‑distillation, exposure to raw data, and privacy-aware or federated KD — yields robust compressed models that approach or match teacher capabilities in practice.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, more efficient students while preserving predictive behavior and, in many cases, improving deployment properties such as latency, memory use, privacy, and robustness. The field has expanded from matching teacher logits to a broad set of signals and workflows — internal feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and selective-sample protocols, meta- and online-teaching schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows that what to transfer (outputs vs. intermediate representations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors), and which data to use (authentic, distilled, augmented, or synthetic) materially affect student outcomes. Practical deployments require task-aware design: align signals to student capacity, mitigate teacher error propagation, handle low-resource or privacy-constrained settings, and combine KD with complementary compression techniques. Remaining challenges include principled theory for which teacher signals are most informative across tasks, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and domain shift, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques that transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD operates via soft-label (logit) transfer, intermediate-feature matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or generative synthesis of data, and many hybrid protocols. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when adapted to task- and data-specific constraints, KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and careful objective design. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression strategy rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. KD spans logits- and feature-based transfers, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and task-specific adaptations. Its strengths include enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, improving latency and memory footprints, and supporting privacy- or data-constrained scenarios. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, data availability and mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, architectural alignment, and deployment heterogeneity require complementary techniques and task-aware engineering to realize reliable, robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single recipe but as a versatile, task-aware toolkit that enables compact, efficient, and deployable models across modalities. KD methods—ranging from logit-based soft targets to feature-, layer-, and relation-level matching, and including self-, multi-teacher, data-free, and online variants—consistently trade small accuracy loss for large gains in latency, memory, and privacy. Reliable application requires careful attention to teacher quality and compatibility, what to transfer, the data regime, and interactions with regularizers and complementary compression methods. When designed around deployment constraints and task objectives, KD delivers practical, often substantial improvements for on-device inference, domain adaptation, federated settings, and robustness-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive and representational information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints such as latency, memory, and privacy. KD has been adapted to diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), multi-teacher schemes, data-free or few-shot regimes, and domain- or task-adaptive pipelines. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student design, KD routinely yields large reductions in model size and runtime while preserving most of the teacher's performance. However, distillation is not automatic: practitioner attention is needed to address teacher selection, data availability and distribution shift, capacity mismatch, low-frequency behavior, and risk of transferring biases or teacher artifacts.

papers_seen.author: Hamilton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to the task, available data, and student capacity, KD can deliver substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving most of the teacher's performance. Success depends on selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, annealing), and how to handle limited or private data (data-free synthesis, adversarial generators, teacher-free regularizers). Although KD is broadly effective, it is not a panacea: failures arise from teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, optimization issues, and transferred biases, motivating targeted protocols and continued research into privacy-aware, robust, and automated distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. Major limitations remain in imperfect belief matching, distribution shift, handling low-frequency phenomena, heterogeneous or privacy-constrained data, and principled teacher selection—areas where methodological and theoretical progress continues to be needed.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or adapts large or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, generative models, and domain- or privacy-constrained settings, a diverse toolbox has been developed—soft-label supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, self- and online-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and architecture-aware adaptations (e.g., pruning, layer skipping, NAS). Empirical results show that appropriately designed KD pipelines can produce compact models that approach teacher performance and enable deployment in resource-constrained environments, while practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and optimization design. Remaining challenges include principled theory linking teacher signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous architectures or non-iid data, privacy-and-fairness-aware protocols, and extending KD to complex generative and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and cross-device constraints when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to align teacher and student. However, its success is conditional: careful selection of teacher signals, attention to data regimes and fairness, and integration with complementary compression methods are required for reliable real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or specialized students to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use a range of objectives — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational losses, adversarially generated supervision, and teacher-free/self-distillation variants — often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective in many settings (supervised, self-supervised, online, federated, and data-free), but its success depends on choices about what information to transfer, teacher quality and alignment to the student, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and the complement of compression techniques used. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both why distillation helps (regularization, privileged information, smoother targets) and when it struggles (capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena), suggesting hybrid pipelines and task-aware designs as practical routes forward.
