papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and cross-device constraints when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to align teacher and student. However, its success is conditional: careful selection of teacher signals, attention to data regimes and fairness, and integration with complementary compression methods are required for reliable real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Practical, but Not Sufficiently Complete Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. KD techniques extend beyond logit matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, attention and projection-based mappings, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-constrained regimes (few-shot, data-free). KD reliably improves deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, and sometimes robustness or privacy), but it has concrete limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, and task-specific design needs—that make KD most effective when integrated with complementary compression and training practices.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for compressing large models and transferring capabilities across domains, modalities, and architectures. When combined with task-aware objectives, careful layer/feature matching, and appropriate data or privacy strategies, KD yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment patterns. KD’s strengths span supervised, self-supervised, online, and privacy-constrained settings, but realizing them requires attention to teacher quality, what knowledge is transferred, and how student capacity and data constraints are handled.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled Toolbox for Practical and Responsible Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that can produce compact, deployable models when combined with complementary design choices. Properly applied—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to map layers, and which auxiliary techniques to use (pretraining, curriculum, adversarial or privacy safeguards)—KD can deliver students that approach or sometimes match teacher performance while enabling latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (data heterogeneity, low-frequency phenomena, imperfect teachers, and optimization challenges) that demand targeted mitigations rather than blind application.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation mimicking, relational or attention-map transfer, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and recommendation settings. Empirical and theoretical work demonstrates substantial practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability when KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping), but success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objective design; remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, distribution shift, rare-token performance, and bias or privacy leakage.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple teacher-to-student logit matching into a broad toolkit for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains. Modern KD transfers soft targets, intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, or synthesized data; it operates in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency, but success depends on teacher quality, capacity matching, data/augmentation strategy, and careful design of objectives and layer mappings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, applications, and practical recommendations documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, evidence-backed approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable models across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD methods — ranging from logits transfer to intermediate-feature matching, self-distillation, and selective-sample protocols — routinely enable substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not automatic: success depends on what information is transferred, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data choices, and integration with complementary compression techniques. When treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline, KD provides a practical route to deploy high-performing models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Necessity, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are essential engineering primitives for making large deep models practical in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, language, and multimodal tasks show that carefully chosen distillation targets, training schedules, and data strategies enable small students to recover much of teacher performance. At the same time, important challenges remain—data heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior preservation, and principled teacher selection—motivating focused research and deployment practices.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Yet Contextual, Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has repeatedly enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across modalities while retaining much of the performance of larger models. Empirical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, inductive biases, and task-specific capabilities from teacher to student, and can be adapted via logit-, feature-, and layer-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial procedures, and data- or privacy-aware variants. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization difficulties, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and propagation of teacher errors limit its effectiveness unless combined with careful protocol design and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as a first-class tool in compression toolkits, but only when used with task-aware filtering, capacity-aware targets, and architecture- or data-aware refinements to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wells
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving protocols, and online/co-distillation schemes—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest accuracy loss when applied with task-aware design. Effective use of KD typically combines careful selection of what to transfer, attention to teacher–student capacity and data regimes, and integration with complementary compression mechanisms such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfection and bias transfer, data scarcity and domain shift, capacity and optimization mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal systems, and specialized domains such as healthcare and novel-view synthesis, KD yields large reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher performance when applied with task-aware design choices. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what information is transferred (logits, features, relational structure), the availability and nature of data, teacher quality and design, and careful integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Pragmatic deployment requires attention to robustness, bias propagation, data scarcity, and domain mismatch, and benefits most from combining KD with task- and hardware-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression encompass a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or richer models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models. Across computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, graph learning, federated settings, and multi-modal systems, KD variants—ranging from feature- and layer-wise matching to self-distillation, data-free adversarial schemes, and task-aware filtering—have been applied to address capacity gaps, domain shifts, privacy constraints, and inference latency. Empirical and methodological work shows that careful alignment between teacher and student (in representation, task relevance, or sample selection), consideration of data heterogeneity, and incorporation of pre-training or auxiliary objectives improve student performance. Open challenges include robust distillation under heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, mitigating bias transfer, and designing distillation objectives that prioritize downstream task relevance while remaining communication- and privacy-efficient.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, detection, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—enable substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, data strategy, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression (e.g., pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Practical deployments use task-aware adaptations, confidence- or curriculum-based weighting, and privacy- or federated-aware designs; remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, rare-output transfer, and principled theory for optimal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Multifaceted Toolbox with Clear Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practically essential approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains and can improve generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods, but it is not a single recipe: success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and constraints such as privacy or heterogeneous deployment hardware. Practical KD pipelines therefore treat distillation as a configurable toolkit—selecting objectives, data strategies, and auxiliary interventions (e.g., pruning, quantization, teacher adaptation, or student-aware design) that match the task and constraints—while explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD techniques extend beyond matching logits: they include internal-representation distillation, adversarial and relational approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware methods, and architecture-aware replacements. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve or even improve generalization, enable domain adaptation, and permit deployment under resource, privacy, or latency constraints—provided practitioners attend to known failure modes such as teacher bias, low-frequency lexical errors, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central and Versatile but Insufficient Alone — Practical Position and Best Practices for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD enables practical deployment across modalities and constrained settings, but its success depends on careful design choices, complementary compression primitives, and explicit safeguards against transferred errors and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically driven framework for transferring predictive and representational information from large or composite teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. The literature shows a broad set of distillation objectives (soft logits, intermediate feature matching, attention and relational transfer, contrastive and adversarial schemes), multiple training protocols (multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free and synthetic-data approaches), and tight integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance in many settings, enable cross-modal and domain adaptation, and produce dramatic runtime and memory gains when applied with task-aware choices of signals, data, and student architectures. Important failure modes remain—teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, data availability and heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns—so best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that must be tailored to the task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Methods span from classic logit-based distillation to feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and projector-based strategies, module-replacement and pruning approaches, and specialized protocols for cross-modal, federated, data-free, and generative settings. Applications range across NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive models), speech and paralinguistic embeddings, vision (image translation, novel-view synthesis), 3D detection, recommender systems, and graph neural networks. Research highlights include analyses that explain why distillation works, techniques that mitigate transfer of teacher errors, curricula and selection mechanisms for better sample usage, and approaches that adapt distillation to privacy- or resource-constrained environments. Together, these works map an ecosystem of practical techniques and open challenges for deploying compact, high-performing models in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a primary practical technique for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD supports a wide variety of goals—reducing latency and memory, enabling on-device inference, preserving privacy when data are unavailable, and transferring robustness or domain knowledge—by varying what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational/contrastive signals) and how training is scheduled (offline, online, progressive replacement, or data-free synthesis). While KD is not a universal cure, its flexibility and empirical success make it a first-choice strategy for compression when combined with careful design choices about teacher quality, transfer signals, and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Methods extend beyond simple teacher-logit matching to include feature and representation alignment, relational objectives, contrastive methods, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling, curriculum and progressive replacement schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware workflows. KD has been successfully applied across vision, language, speech, graph-structured data, retrieval, and constrained-device deployments, and is commonly combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency and memory budgets. Key practical concerns include what to transfer, how to cope with teacher-student mismatch and limited or private data, optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, and measurement of distilled model robustness and fairness. While empirical progress has been large and diverse, theoretical and systems-level problems remain active areas of research.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit — from soft-label matching to representation-level, adversarial, and data-free approaches — has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. Practical success depends on careful choice of distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable models while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature shows a wide range of KD mechanisms (logit- and feature-based losses, adversarial and data-free schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols) and application domains (NLP, vision, multimodal, detection, federated settings). KD succeeds best when combined with complementary practices—pretraining, layer-wise alignment, data augmentation, teacher adaptation, and hardware-aware compression—but it faces limitations from teacher errors, data absence, distributional mismatch, and heterogeneous deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature-, attention- and layer-wise alignment, relational/contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, and meta- or multi-teacher schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, retrieval, graph, and federated settings. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with task- and architecture-aware design choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization stability; proposed remedies emphasize task-aware filtering of teacher signals, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.
