papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for compressing large models and transferring capabilities across domains, modalities, and architectures. When combined with task-aware objectives, careful layer/feature matching, and appropriate data or privacy strategies, KD yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment patterns. KD’s strengths span supervised, self-supervised, online, and privacy-constrained settings, but realizing them requires attention to teacher quality, what knowledge is transferred, and how student capacity and data constraints are handled.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature collectively reports about knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques: commonly used distillation objectives and training protocols, empirical patterns of when and how KD helps across modalities, practical constraints and failure modes (data availability, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency/structured outputs, privacy and bias transfer), and targeted solutions (data-free/zero-shot distillation, teacher engineering, multi-teacher and curriculum schemes, and combinations with pruning/quantization and architecture search). The goal is to give a concise map of methods, observed trade-offs, and open problems for researchers and practitioners working on compressing or adapting large models for resource- or deployment-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It enables deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints across vision, language, and multimodal tasks while supporting robustness and transfer when combined with task-aware design. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and data quality, architectural alignment, and complementary compression techniques, and it can propagate teacher biases and fail on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena unless mitigated.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster students to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and compute. A diverse set of distillation targets and training paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention-map imitation, layer-wise mapping, adversarial and data-free generation of surrogate examples, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and integration with architecture search or pruning—have been developed and adapted to vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of the teacher's accuracy (and in some settings improves generalization or robustness) when combined with task-aware choices of signals to transfer, data augmentation, and teacher-student design; remaining gaps and failure modes are linked to teacher quality, data availability and distribution shift, heterogeneous architectures, and fairness or robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers predictive ability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, efficient student models. Across modalities and architectures, KD variants extend beyond matching teacher output probabilities to include internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, adversarial learning, selective sample supervision, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. These methods enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, reduce inference latency, support domain adaptation and federated settings, and in some cases improve student generalization beyond the teacher. Practical challenges include input/representation mismatches between teacher and student, propagation of teacher biases (e.g., low-frequency lexical errors), and the need for careful selection of what is distilled and how. Empirically, tailored distillation objectives and training procedures—such as internal-representation matching, progressive module replacement, ensemble distillation, and contrastive or relational objectives—have produced strong compression results across vision, language, graph-structured data, and generative scene models.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across logits-based soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, layer-mapping or projector modules, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or federated protocols, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical results show KD can sometimes improve generalization and enable deployment under privacy or resource constraints, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and careful design choices about what and how to transfer. Combining KD with complementary techniques (augmentation, curriculum learning, pruning, quantization, architecture search) and tailoring the distillation signals to task and deployment constraints yields the most reliable practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is now a central, broadly applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and functional behavior of larger teachers. The literature describes a rich taxonomy of KD objectives and protocols — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures — together with specialized strategies for online, multi-teacher, data-free, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often improves student generalization and acts as a regularizer, but success depends on task-aware choices: which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of teacher errors or low-frequency behaviors. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and augmentation strategies, and targeted safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Practices, Mechanisms, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of methods for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD techniques vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure), how teachers and students are arranged (offline, online, ensemble, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers), and whether distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD succeeds across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks but is context-sensitive: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, loss and mapping design, and deployment constraints. Practical distillation therefore requires task- and deployment-aware choices, and often additional techniques (data augmentation, feature projectors, adversarial objectives, or data-free synthesis) to close the gap to teachers while avoiding transferred errors or degraded handling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable models across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When paired with complementary techniques—layer mapping, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, pruning/quantization, and curriculum or online schemes—KD yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance while supporting privacy-conscious and latency-constrained deployments. Remaining limits around data availability, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional mismatch can be mitigated by choosing appropriate distillation targets and architectures and by combining KD with targeted engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the capabilities of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of techniques for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving task performance. Across vision, language, and multimodal domains, KD has evolved beyond logits-only supervision into rich protocols that match intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized data or generator-based replay. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful objective and layer alignment. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, practical recommendations, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment across domains and modalities. When designed with task-awareness (choice of distilled signal, teacher selection, and training scheme), KD can preserve accuracy while materially improving latency, memory, and privacy characteristics. Best results arise from combining multiple KD techniques (logit, feature, layer-wise, adversarial, and ensemble-based) chosen to match the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD has been shown to work across modalities and tasks by transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure. It can also be combined with data augmentation, adversarial schemes, online or teacher-free training, and architecture-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints. KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about which teacher signals to transfer, alignment of inputs and architectures, student capacity, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. When used as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that addresses these issues, KD delivers substantial practical benefits for latency- and resource-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers that preserves much of their performance across tasks and modalities. Its strengths arise from multiple transfer mechanisms (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and from compatibility with complementary compression tools. However, KD is not automatic: success requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and integration with other compression methods. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of modern model-deployment toolkits, with explicit practices to mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving much of task performance. KD is a flexible family of techniques that operate at output, representation, relational, or decision-boundary levels and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful design of objectives and training pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical framework for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving functionality across modalities. When combined with task-aware choices of distilled signals, data strategies, and complementary compression methods, KD enables large reductions in model size and latency with modest performance loss and can also address privacy, robustness, and deployment constraints. However, KD has failure modes — including propagation of teacher biases, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shifts — that require targeted remedies. Careful design, including multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, exposure to raw or synthesized data, and joint optimization with pruning or architecture search, makes KD an indispensable component of practical model-deployment toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are now core tools for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. The literature has expanded far beyond simple logits matching to include feature- and representation-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, and tight integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates broad applicability across modalities (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and generative models) and deployment contexts (edge devices, federated systems, and data-constrained settings). The main practical challenges are (1) choosing what and how to distill for a given task and student architecture, (2) coping with limited or unavailable original training data, (3) avoiding transfer of teacher weaknesses (e.g., biases or low-frequency degradation), and (4) co-designing distillation with other compression primitives and hardware constraints. Progress comes from combining representational objectives, layer-mapping strategies, task-aware teacher selection, and safeguards (privacy or fairness) appropriate to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have evolved from a simple teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a broad toolbox for producing compact, efficient, and adaptable models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research has produced a range of practical methods—logit and feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware variants, and federated or online protocols—and has clarified connections to regularization, ensemble learning, and optimization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of the teacher's performance, though gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and adaptation to deployment constraints. This synthesis summarizes core methods, theoretical insights, empirical findings, practical considerations, and open challenges that shape current best practice for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers across vision, language, graph, recommendation, and generative settings. KD encompasses a range of techniques—soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, layer- and channel-wise mappings, and data- or task-aware variants—and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can enable deployable, lower-latency models, improve robustness and interpretability in some settings, and serve as a substrate for domain adaptation and privacy-aware workflows; its success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and practical engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Multifaceted Toolbox with Clear Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practically essential approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains and can improve generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods, but it is not a single recipe: success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and constraints such as privacy or heterogeneous deployment hardware. Practical KD pipelines therefore treat distillation as a configurable toolkit—selecting objectives, data strategies, and auxiliary interventions (e.g., pruning, quantization, teacher adaptation, or student-aware design) that match the task and constraints—while explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative tasks. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, features, attention, or generated data), data strategy, and teacher–student alignment, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory gains while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, so it is best used as part of an integrated compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core set of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and layer correspondences; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search. KD supports many practical settings — including data-limited, data-free, few-shot, federated, and cross-modal scenarios — but its effectiveness depends on choices such as which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Ongoing directions include principled theory for transfer objectives, robust and private distillation, and task-aware designs for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and sometimes improve robustness or task adaptation. A diverse toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and generative data-free techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and selective or meta-learned teaching—and empirical and theoretical work clarifies when and why these choices succeed or fail. Practical deployment requires matching the distilled signal to student capacity and task constraints, handling data- or architecture-mismatch, and explicitly addressing bias and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are essential for deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints. Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and NLP shows that combining sensible pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals (outputs and internal representations), appropriate training data or augmentation, and dynamic teacher-student strategies yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Complementary techniques — online or mutual distillation, data-free and federated distillation, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation — further extend applicability to privacy-constrained, multi-domain, and large-scale training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD methods vary by what is transferred (teacher logits, internal representations, attention, relational structure), how layers are aligned or projected, and how data constraints (limited access, privacy, or distribution shift) are handled. Empirical work demonstrates that combining output-level and representation-level objectives, using layer-mapping or projector modules, and adapting training data or curricula yields the best trade-offs between compactness and accuracy. Despite wide success, effective distillation requires careful choices about teacher quality, distilled signals, sample selection, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from teacher models. Across tasks and modalities, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and structure-preserving objectives—enable deployable models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory use, and communication cost. Distillation also serves as a flexible substrate for addressing domain adaptation, lifelong learning, robustness, low-precision deployment, and generator compression. However, realizing these benefits in practice requires careful design choices around what to transfer, how to map layers and representations, how to handle limited or private teacher data, and how to mitigate bias or robustness loss.
