papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Evidence, Methods, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while often preserving much of teacher performance. A large body of work develops variants that match logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, supports multi-teacher and teacher‑free regimes, and combines distillation with data augmentation, adversarial synthesis, or architectural adaptations. Despite robust practical gains, important open problems remain in data‑scarce or privacy‑constrained distillation, transferring fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping for heterogeneous architectures, and fairness- and robustness-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Practices, Mechanisms, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of methods for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD techniques vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure), how teachers and students are arranged (offline, online, ensemble, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers), and whether distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD succeeds across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks but is context-sensitive: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, loss and mapping design, and deployment constraints. Practical distillation therefore requires task- and deployment-aware choices, and often additional techniques (data augmentation, feature projectors, adversarial objectives, or data-free synthesis) to close the gap to teachers while avoiding transferred errors or degraded handling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core method for producing compact, efficient models from large deep networks across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD delivers substantial inference and memory savings while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, enabling deployment in latency-, power-, and privacy-constrained settings. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections (biases, distributional blind spots) and faces practical constraints (data mismatch, teacher–student capacity gaps, limited-data regimes). Effective use of KD therefore requires matching objectives, data strategies, and architectures to deployment goals and complementing distillation with pruning, quantization, or privacy-aware protocols when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A synthesis of methods, evidence, and practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, multifaceted toolkit for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. The field unifies a set of objectives (soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational/contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, self- and mutual-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-annealed schedules), and data strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis, adversarial generation) that, when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable effective deployment across vision, language, generative modelling, and domain- and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical evidence demonstrates strong gains when distillation is matched to student capacity, teacher quality, and appropriate data/augmentation strategies, but persistent challenges remain in data-scarce, privacy-sensitive, domain-shift, and heterogeneous-architecture regimes.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster, or specialized student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad and practical toolbox has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free/zero-shot protocols, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search—that is applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative settings. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when applied carefully, but success depends on student capacity, teacher design/quality, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices; important open problems remain in principled theory, fairness/privacy-aware protocols, heterogeneous and federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Vance
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component: The Case for Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applied method for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller students. KD variants (logits, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free and federated protocols) have enabled practical deployment across vision, language, retrieval, generative modeling, and healthcare. However, KD faces concrete limitations—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and potential fairness or robustness regressions—that reduce its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest practical outcomes come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful selection or synthesis of distilled supervision, and task- and data-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones into a broad set of methods that address efficiency, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness, fairness, and cross-modal transfer. By moving beyond simple logits matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher schemes, data-free and few-shot settings, and meta-learned teachers, distillation can both preserve performance and add functional guarantees (e.g., robustness, fairness) that are crucial for real-world deployment. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be considered a foundational component of model compression pipelines and of strategies for adapting large pre-trained models to constrained, specialized, or sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and latency while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. Its strengths derive from a broad family of techniques—soft-target/logit matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, adversarial or contrastive data synthesis, online co-training, and data-free/zero-shot synthesis—combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal panacea: careful, task-aware choices about which signals to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to handle limited or private data are essential to avoid pitfalls like bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, and teacher–student mismatch. Treating KD as a configurable toolbox—integrated with pretraining, augmentation, and evaluation practices—yields the best outcomes for practical deployment and research progress.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, structured prediction, and language tasks—KD variants (logit transfer, feature- and attention-matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols) provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as architecture search, pruning, low-precision numerics, or privacy mechanisms, distillation enables robust deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive platforms. However, distillation outcomes depend on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student alignment, and design choices for objectives and training pipelines; tailored practices are therefore needed to realize KD's full potential and avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression encompass a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or richer models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models. Across computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, graph learning, federated settings, and multi-modal systems, KD variants—ranging from feature- and layer-wise matching to self-distillation, data-free adversarial schemes, and task-aware filtering—have been applied to address capacity gaps, domain shifts, privacy constraints, and inference latency. Empirical and methodological work shows that careful alignment between teacher and student (in representation, task relevance, or sample selection), consideration of data heterogeneity, and incorporation of pre-training or auxiliary objectives improve student performance. Open challenges include robust distillation under heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, mitigating bias transfer, and designing distillation objectives that prioritize downstream task relevance while remaining communication- and privacy-efficient.

papers_seen.author: Sims
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A broad toolkit has emerged — including logits/soft-label transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search — enabling deployment across vision, speech, language, generative, and multimodal settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in latency, memory, calibration, and sometimes robustness, while pointing to failure modes driven by teacher quality, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and distribution shift; best practice treats KD as a core element of a broader, context-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Evidence, Methods, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while often preserving much of teacher performance. A large body of work develops variants that match logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, supports multi-teacher and teacher‑free regimes, and combines distillation with data augmentation, adversarial synthesis, or architectural adaptations. Despite robust practical gains, important open problems remain in data‑scarce or privacy‑constrained distillation, transferring fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping for heterogeneous architectures, and fairness- and robustness-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, researchers have extended KD beyond soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, online and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. Practical success depends on teacher quality and student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthetic-data strategies, and combinations with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include principled understanding of when particular signals help, handling heterogeneous or non-iid data in federated settings, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and reliably scaling distillation in large distributed systems.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically driven framework for transferring predictive and representational information from large or composite teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. The literature shows a broad set of distillation objectives (soft logits, intermediate feature matching, attention and relational transfer, contrastive and adversarial schemes), multiple training protocols (multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free and synthetic-data approaches), and tight integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance in many settings, enable cross-modal and domain adaptation, and produce dramatic runtime and memory gains when applied with task-aware choices of signals, data, and student architectures. Important failure modes remain—teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, data availability and heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns—so best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that must be tailored to the task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD has matured into a toolbox that includes logit- and feature-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free and adversarial generation, online and multi-teacher schemes, and task-aware layer alignment. Its effectiveness in reducing parameters, latency, and memory—often with modest performance loss—makes KD a core first-line method for deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, bias transfer, limited or private data) that require task-aware protocols, complementary compression techniques, and targeted research into robustness, privacy, and automated teacher/student design.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for transferring predictive behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. KD spans logits-based supervision, feature and relational matching, adversarial or synthetic data generation, and architectural or curriculum adaptations. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD can enable deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings and sometimes yield students that match or exceed teacher performance, but it also carries risks—propagating teacher errors and biases, struggling under data scarcity or mismatch, and requiring task-specific engineering. I argue KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines, applied conditionally with targeted remedies and validated against task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide flexible, broadly applicable ways to transfer performance from large teacher models to compact student models so they can run under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, relational signals) and procedures (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, meta-learned teachers, data-free synthesis) have been developed and integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, ensembling). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and recommendation systems shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve deployability, though success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Remaining directions include automated, task-adaptive transfer choices, robust data-free distillation, and principled controls for fairness and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.
